extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and evaluating obviousness analyses under 35 U.S.C. 103, including how to compare prior art to claimed inventions, assess inherency and teachings-away, and determine the appropriate level of ordinary skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claimed invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the differences between the prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the claim language and consider both the invention and the prior art references as a whole; do not focus improperly on isolated structural differences (see Stratoflex, Schenck v. Nortron, In re Hirao).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust'
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' of an invention disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating an invention as if it reads differently than allowed by ignoring express claim limitations (see W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb, Jones v. Hardy, Panduit). Consider all claim limitations and their effect on obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of the source/cause of a problem is part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable invention may lie in the discovery of the source of a problem even though the remedy may be obvious once the source is identified; this discovery is part of the subject matter 'as a whole' to be considered under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat discovery of a problem's source as potentially patentable subject matter, but recognize that if the prior art already contains the same solution for a similar problem the invention may still be obvious (see In re Sponnoble; distinguishing In re Wiseman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants alleging discovery must provide substantiating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants who allege the inventor discovered the source of a problem must provide evidence substantiating the allegation (affidavits/declarations or clear and persuasive assertions in the specification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsubstantiated statements (e.g., counsel argument) are insufficient. Evidence must support the claim that the inventor discovered the cause and that this discovery is reflected in the disclosure (see In re Wiseman; In re Kaslow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include disclosed inherent properties in the 'as a whole' analysis (inherency)
rubrics_metrics.description: In delineating the invention as a whole, look not only to the subject matter literally recited in the claim but also to those properties inherent in the subject matter and disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider inherent properties when they are disclosed in the specification (In re Antonie). Note that after KSR, a known result-effective variable may motivate experimentation but is not alone determinative; do not predicate obviousness on features not known at the relevant time (see In re Rijckaert and MPEP §2112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base obviousness on features not known at the relevant time
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness cannot be predicated on what is not known at the relevant time, even if inherency of a certain feature is later established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the feature or property relied upon to show obviousness was known or disclosed at the relevant time (see In re Rijckaert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prior art in its entirety, including teachings that teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference must be considered as a whole, including portions that would lead away from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If portions of the art teach away from the claimed invention, combining that art with others may not render the claim obvious (see W.L. Gore example). However, merely disclosing multiple alternatives in a reference does not automatically constitute teaching away (see In re Fulton). Consider simultaneous advantages/disadvantages do not necessarily negate a motivation to combine (Allied Erecting v. Genesis Attachments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in determining the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors may include: (A) type of problems encountered in the art; (B) prior art solutions to those problems; (C) rapidity with which innovations are made; (D) sophistication of the technology; and (E) educational level of active workers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every factor will be present in every case and one or more may predominate. Use these factors (In re GPAC; Custom Accessories; Environmental Designs) to inform the hypothetical person's capabilities when assessing obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill is a person of ordinary creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of ordinary skill in the art is also a person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that such a person can fit teachings of multiple patents together and employ inferences and creative steps; examiners may consider what inferences and creative steps would be employed (KSR v. Teleflex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification disclosure (or silence) may inform the level of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of disclosure in the specification or in relevant references may be informative of the knowledge and skills of a person of ordinary skill in the art; specification silence on how to achieve a step may suggest that achieving it was within ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specification content (or its silence) as evidence of what a person of ordinary skill would know, provided the specification complies with 35 U.S.C. 112 (see Uber Techs. v. X One).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical skilled person is defined by capability, not credentials alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothetical 'person having ordinary skill in the art' must have the capability of understanding the scientific and engineering principles applicable to the pertinent art and is not definable solely by credentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a specific high credential (e.g., doctorate) unless the record supports that definition; the evidence in the application must support any asserted high level of credentials (Ex parte Hiyamizu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-prior-art contemporaneous materials can inform skill level and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: References which are not prior art may nevertheless be relied upon to demonstrate the level of ordinary skill in the art and to show motivation to combine implicit in the knowledge of one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporaneous invention, internal materials, or drawings may be probative of knowledge in the art and motivation to combine even if not technically prior art (In re Merck; Ecolochem; Thomas & Betts; Nat'l Steel Car).

rubrics_metrics.name: When prior art itself reflects the appropriate skill level, specifying a skill level may be unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only facts of record pertaining to the level of skill are found within the prior art of record, an invention may be held obvious without a specific finding of a particular level of skill where the prior art itself reflects an appropriate level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the prior art to reflect the level of ordinary skill where appropriate (Chore-Time Equipment v. Cumberland; Okajima v. Bourdeau).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain level of ordinary skill to maintain objectivity in obviousness inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art is necessary to maintain objectivity in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must determine what would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time — not to the inventor, judge, layman, remote-arts practitioners, or geniuses (Ryko Mfg. Co. v. Nu-Star; Environmental Designs).
